common_name: Great Lakes Bearded Iris (Historic Dykes Medal Blue Self)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, with the top surface exposed to the sun, in late summer to early fall; Great Lakes is a historic tall bearded iris that won the American Iris Society's Dykes Medal in 1942 and remains a benchmark true-blue self.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun, never buried, in well-drained soil. Registered by L.W. Cousins in 1938 and named for its origin near the Great Lakes region of Canada, this tall bearded iris bears clear, pure medium-blue self flowers of excellent form and substance on strong, well-branched stems, with a fragrance reminiscent of magnolia. It was the top-ranked iris in the American Iris Society's annual symposium for four consecutive years and won the Dykes Medal in 1942, later entering the AIS Hall of Fame as one of the most influential blue tall beardeds of the mid-20th century. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom, discarding the older woody center and replanting healthy outer fans; good drainage is essential, since standing moisture causes rhizome rot far more readily than this iris is bothered by drought.

common_name: Dominion Bearded Iris (Historic Foundational Neglecta Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, with the top surface exposed to the sun, in late summer to early fall; Dominion is a historic 1917 tall bearded iris considered the single most influential cultivar in the creation of modern tetraploid bearded irises.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil, never burying them completely. Bred by English hybridizer Arthur J. Bliss and introduced in 1917, Dominion is a neglecta-pattern iris with light bluish-violet standards and falls of exceptional velvety substance in deep indigo-purple, held on strong stems above broad, heavy-textured petals unlike anything seen in bearded iris before it. Its breeding launched a decade-long flood of new introductions in the 1920s, and historians of the genus have credited Dominion as the pivotal cultivar without which modern tetraploid tall bearded iris breeding would not have developed as it did. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom to maintain vigor, and keep rhizomes in full sun with excellent drainage, since standing water quickly causes rot.

common_name: Souvenir de Mme Gaudichau Bearded Iris (Historic French Velvety Dark Purple)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, with the top surface exposed to the sun, in late summer to early fall; Souvenir de Mme Gaudichau is a fragrant, historic French tall bearded iris introduced in 1914 and still grown by heirloom iris collectors.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil, never burying them completely. Registered by the French nursery Millet et Fils in 1914, this early-midseason tall bearded iris carries richly fragrant, velvety flowers with violet standards over blackish-purple falls accented by a blue-and-gold beard, described in period catalogs as among the largest and finest dark purple irises of its era. It became an important parent of later dark-toned cultivars and remains prized today for its old-fashioned form, heavy substance, and strong perfume. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom to maintain vigor, and keep rhizomes in full sun with excellent drainage, since standing water quickly causes rot.

common_name: Snow Flurry Bearded Iris (Historic Ruffled White Parent Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, with the top surface exposed to the sun, in late summer to early fall; Snow Flurry is a historic 1939 ruffled white tall bearded iris that became a foundational parent behind decades of later white and blue cultivars.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil, never burying them completely. Registered by Clara Rees in 1939 from a cross of 'Purissima' and 'Thais', Snow Flurry bears sweetly fragrant, heavily ruffled, semi-flaring flowers of pure ice-white with the faintest blue cast, carried in abundance on well-branched stems that can hold up to a dozen or more blooms per stalk. It won an AIS Award of Merit in 1949 and became one of the most influential parent plants in iris history, standing behind countless later whites and blues, including 'New Snow' and its own descendant 'Cliffs of Dover'. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom to maintain vigor, and keep rhizomes in full sun with excellent drainage, since standing water quickly causes rot.

common_name: Cliffs of Dover Bearded Iris (Historic Opaque White Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, with the top surface exposed to the sun, in late summer to early fall; Cliffs of Dover is a historic 1952 tall bearded iris prized for its unusually intense, chalky-opaque white flowers.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil, never burying them completely. Registered by Orville Fay in 1952 from a cross of 'New Snow' and 'Cahokia', Cliffs of Dover produces midseason flowers of an unusually intense, chalky-opaque white that inspired its name, evoking the famous English coastline. It earned an AIS Award of Merit in 1955 and has remained a garden and hybridizing favorite for its clean color and dependable performance. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom to maintain vigor, and keep rhizomes in full sun with excellent drainage, since standing water quickly causes rot.

common_name: Bottle Rocket Bearded Iris (Dykes Medal Reblooming Orange-Red Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Bottle Rocket won the American Iris Society's Dykes Medal in 2019.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun, never buried, in well-drained soil; soggy conditions cause rhizome rot far more readily than this iris is bothered by drought. Bred by Michael Sutton and registered in 2009, Bottle Rocket bears striking orange-buff standards flushed pink at the midribs above ruby-red falls veined orange and rimmed in a fine greyed-orange border, with bright orange beards nestled amid white spray; blooms carry a light musky fragrance and the plant reblooms later in the season in many climates. It earned the American Iris Society's Wister Medal in 2018 and the top Dykes Medal in 2019, cementing its place among the most acclaimed warm-colored tall beardeds of its era. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom, discarding the older woody center and replanting healthy outer fans.

Bred by Keith Keppel and registered in 2007, Montmartre displays a striking luminata pattern: greyed red-purple standards edged in straw yellow sit above velvety dark red-purple falls with a narrow oyster-white rim, lemon-yellow haft, and chrome-yellow beards tipped white and lemon. It earned the American Iris Society's Wister Medal in 2014 and the top Dykes Medal in 2017, ranking it among the most acclaimed pattern irises of the 21st century.
